strengths: Rigorous real-world validation with 2,000+ robot rollouts across 4 diverse bimanual tasks, providing strong empirical evidence for the approach with Wilson confidence intervals and stage-wise analysis.

Comprehensive and well-designed ablation studies (Tables 5 & 7) that effectively validate core design choices, especially the pathway swapping experiment showing dramatic performance drops when modality assignments are changed.
Practical and parameter-efficient tactile adapter achieving comparable performance to training from scratch (DECO.ds) while updating only 8.7% of parameters, demonstrating genuine efficiency gains.

Clear actionable insights distinguishing weakly vs. strongly tactile-relevant tasks, with quantified improvements (20% on contact-rich tasks) that guide practitioners on when tactile sensing is worthwhile.
Addresses a genuine gap in available datasets: DECO-50 is the first large-scale bimanual dexterous manipulation dataset with tactile sensing on real robots, valuable for the community.
Excellent reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters, comprehensive supplementary material (per-object results, data statistics, data collection methodology), and promised code/data release.
Sound technical methodology with correct flow-matching loss formulation and appropriate experimental controls including statistical testing and out-of-distribution evaluation.
weaknesses: Limited generalization scope: Single hardware platform (Unitree H1-2 with Inspire RH56DFTP hands) and single tactile sensor modality (piezoresistive, normal force only). Generalization to other dexterous hands and tactile technologies is entirely unknown.

Incremental algorithmic novelty: Core components (DiT, AdaLN, cross-attention, LoRA) are all existing techniques. The contribution is primarily their combination and modality assignment, which is sensible but engineering-focused rather than providing fundamental algorithmic innovation.

Mixed simulation results weaken generalization claims: LIBERO 94.2% (tied with π0), RoboTwin 2.0 85.3% (3 points behind baselines), UniVTAC 82.1% (behind N0-VTLA). Vision-only DECO does not consistently outperform baselines across benchmarks, suggesting benefits may be task-specific.

Baseline selection concerns: Primary comparisons are against ACT (2023) and DP (2025). Contemporary methods (π0, π0.5) often outperform DECO on simulation benchmarks, and the 21% improvement is relative to weaker baselines with 51-57% base success rates.

Dataset scale is modest: DECO-50 has only 50 hours and 8K trajectories compared to RoboMIND 2.0 (1000+ hours) and Open X-Embodiment (1M+ episodes), though the value lies in the specific modality combination rather than absolute scale.

Weak out-of-distribution generalization: Material sorting Task 2 OOD results show drastic drops (DECO: 4/20 on black mouse vs 20/20 on training objects), suggesting limited robustness to distribution shifts.

UniVTAC tactile improvements are marginal: The tactile adapter only shifts slip failures minimally (6→4 on insert_tube, 37→41 on insert_hole) with 82.1% average unchanged. Insert_HDMI failures remain timeout-based, suggesting the problem may not be solvable by tactile information.

Limited analysis of learned representations: While the paper identifies when tactile helps, deeper analysis of what tactile signal features are learned and how they influence decision-making would strengthen understanding.

Two-stage training justification unclear: No ablation comparing joint training (vision + tactile from scratch) vs. two-stage training is provided, leaving the motivation for the training paradigm implicit.

strengths: Strong real-world validation with 2,000+ robot rollouts across four tasks demonstrates practical viability
Convincing ablation studies (Tables 5, 7) prove that decoupled multimodal conditioning outperforms naive coupling and that specific pathway assignments are crucial
Well-motivated architecture with clear task-dependent analysis showing when tactile sensing is beneficial (14-18% gains on contact-rich tasks)
Parameter-efficient tactile adapter achieves performance comparable to training from scratch while tuning only ~10% of parameters
Comprehensive supplementary material with detailed hyperparameters, per-object results with Wilson confidence intervals, and code/dataset release promise
Clear nuanced finding that different modalities contribute unequally—pick-and-place and sorting see modest tactile gains (2-4%) while assembly and waste disposal benefit significantly (14-18%)
Good presentation with effective figures and clear problem formulation motivating decoupled conditioning approach
weaknesses: Evaluation restricted to single hardware platform (Unitree H1-2, Inspire RH56DFTP hand) severely limits generalization claims—no cross-embodiment validation despite community focus on embodiment-agnostic approaches

Architectural novelty is incremental: combines existing techniques (DiT, LoRA, AdaLN, cross-attention) with intuitive but unsurprising insight that different modalities should use different conditioning pathways
DECO-50 dataset (50 hours, 8K trajectories) substantially smaller than contemporaries (DROID: 350h, RoboMIND 2.0: 1000+ hours), limiting utility for pretraining and skill breadth

Mixed simulation results undermine generalization claims: LIBERO (tied with π0), RoboTwin 2.0 (3% behind baselines), UniVTAC (zero tactile benefit), DexJoCo (modest 3.9% advantage)—tactile adapter provides no improvement on UniVTAC despite strong real-world gains
Tactile sensor measures only normal force without shear/tangential components, limiting information richness and applicability to richer manipulation scenarios
Limited to four controlled lab tasks (pick-and-place, sorting, waste disposal, assembly)—generalization to more complex, long-horizon, or unstructured manipulation tasks unclear
Out-of-distribution generalization shows significant performance drops (Table 14: OOD on Material Sorting) deserving deeper analysis
Baseline comparison uses modified DP channel configuration [256, 512, 1024] vs original [512, 1024, 2048], complicating direct comparison despite stated justification
Tactile encoder design (Eq. 4) is straightforward linear gating with sigmoid—not particularly sophisticated; similar adapter approaches explored in concurrent work (Higuera et al., 2025)
